summary: Edward Cattell was a farm hand at Kirkwood and a friend of the Staffords, and Whitman met him in May 1876 at the same farm where he was spending his summers with Harry Stafford. Whitman's diaries record the front gate at night in June, the boys swimming, September meetings by the pond on moonlight nights. In January 1877 Whitman wrote asking him to keep away from the Stafford house altogether, to ask no questions and tell no one - the same letter in which he writes 'as to Harry you know how I love him' and then, of Cattell, 'you too have my unalterable love'. Cattell, husking corn that October, wrote back that he had seen Whitman's old chair floating down the stream. He is the poorest-documented man on this map with letters on both sides, and no one recorded when he was born or when he died.

sources.quote:
Dear Ed

I want to write you a few lines particular. Do not call to see me any more at the Stafford family, & do not call there at all any more. Dont ask me why—I will explain to you when we meet. … I want you to keep this to yourself, & not mention it nor this letter to any one & you must not speak about it at all to any one.

There is nothing in it that I think I do wrong, nor am ashamed of, but I wish it kept entirely between you and me … Mr and Mrs Stafford are very near & kind to me, & have been & are like brother & sister to me—& as to Harry you know how I love him. Ed you too have my unalterable love, & always shall have.
sources.context: Whitman to Cattell, 24 January 1877 - **a draft; the sent version has not been found**. The elision drops instructions to treat the Staffords normally in public. The archive records that Whitman deleted, and then rewrote in different words, the sentence about the Staffords and Harry, and deleted an invitation to be visited at Mrs Gilchrist's house in Philadelphia. Read alongside cattell's reply and the stafford--whitman edge: Whitman is managing two attachments in the same household and asking one of them to become invisible.
sources.supports: Whitman's own declaration of love to Cattell, and - in the same breath - the concealment it was conducted under.

sources.quote:
old man i got your kind and welcom letter last week and was glad to hear from you my loving old friend i love to hear from you and to know that you ar well and i would Com up to see you But i cant get of a day now for we ar so Bisse now husking corn i went with some Boys up the Pond to day and i seen your old Chir floting down the stream … i think of you old man think of the times down on the Crieek. … i love you Walt and all ways will so may god Bless you

is my prayer from of your frend

Edward P Cattell
sources.context: Cattell to Whitman, 21 October 1877, headed only 'Sunday 21th'. **The spelling and capitalisation are Cattell's own** and are preserved here as the archive preserves them; he was a farm labourer and wrote as he could. The elisions drop his news of George Stafford and Herbert Gilchrist and his hope of coming to Camden. Recorded in full register rather than trimmed to the declaration, because trimming it to 'i love you Walt' would tidy away the husking and the floating chair, which are the texture of the thing.
sources.supports: Cattell's own voice - the only substantial thing of his that survives, and the other half of the self-reported class.

null_findings.finding: NO DATES EXIST FOR CATTELL in anything consulted, and this is a finding rather than a gap in the search. Stafford and Doyle each have a signed reference entry with birth and death years in its title; Cattell has none, and the nearest the record comes is Whitman's own note that he was 'about 25 or 6' in 1876. He is a farm labourer, and the apparatus that records dates - articles, entries, obituaries, portraits - tracks property. The `born` and `died` fields are therefore null by evidence, not by oversight. The diary and commonplace-book entries the archive quotes ('the hour (night, June 19, '76, Ed & I.) at the front gate by the road'; 'Sept meetings Ed C by the pond at Kirkwood moonlight nights') are in the Feinberg Collection at the Library of Congress - they are quoted here only as the archive quotes them, and remain the obvious next step.
